data.title: US Senate fails to advance sweeping cryptocurrency bill in blow for industry
data.description:
(Corrects paragraph 2 to say Senator Collins, not Senator Paul, voted against the bill)

By Hannah Lang

Sept 15 (Reuters) - The U.S. Senate failed on Tuesday to advance comprehensive cryptocurrency legislation backed by ‌President Donald Trump in a major blow for digital asset companies and Republicans who had championed ‌the bill for months.

The bill, called the Clarity Act, fell 10 short of reaching the 60-vote threshold needed to advance most legislation ​in the 100-seat chamber, as four Republican senators — Jerry Moran, Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Thom Tillis — joined all the Democrats in voting against it. The vote was 50-49 in favor.

The vote effectively put the bill on ice, as Congress is set to depart Washington this month ahead of the November midterm elections in which Trump's fellow ‌Republicans are fighting to retain control ⁠of the House of Representatives and Senate.

Tillis switched his vote from yes to no in a procedural move that preserves his ability to bring the measure back up for ⁠reconsideration later.

Senate Republicans on Sunday night released a new text of the bill in a last-ditch effort to address concerns from the banking industry and some Democrats, but the opponents were not swayed.

The Clarity Act aimed to create a ​regulatory framework ​for digital assets, which crypto companies say would put ​them on a more solid legal footing. The ‌deep-pocketed industry spent hundreds of millions of dollars campaigning to advance the bill.

Trump, who has earned more than $1.4 billion from his family's crypto ventures, had urged Congress to pass it. Trump courted cash from the crypto industry on the campaign trail during the 2024 election, calling himself a "crypto president."

His regulators, particularly the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, will now be positioned to fill the crypto policy void, ‌but efforts to write favorable rules for the digital asset ​industry could prove challenging.

Industry experts have said that only Congress can ​create a lasting regulatory framework. Without legislation, regulations ​will be vulnerable to the shifting political climate and court challenges, creating lingering hazards ‌for the crypto industry, said executives and analysts.

The ​Trump administration's own extensive rollback ​of dozens of SEC and consumer watchdog policies introduced under former Democratic President Joe Biden has underscored that risk.

Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5% as the vote appeared on track ​to fail, its biggest daily percentage ‌decline since June. Shares of crypto exchange Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle fell as much as ​10%.

(Reporting by Hannah Lang in New York; Additional reporting by Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss in New York; ​Editing by Matthew Lewis, Will Dunham and Hugh Lawson)

data.title: The US military said it has deployed weapons in space. Here’s what that could mean
data.description:
The US military said it has deployed weapons in space. Here’s what that could mean

Hanna Park, Jackie Wattles, CNN
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:22 pm UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The United States has deployed weapons in space and will use them to defend American forces, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday. It's the first public acknowledgment that the nation has such capabilities in orbit and a potential signal to those that could pose threats in the domain.

"Today we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist," Meink told attendees of the Air, Space and Cyber Conference, an annual gathering hosted by the Air & Space Forces Association in National Harbor, Maryland. "This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action."

Meink did not provide specifics on the weapons and, when asked to expand, refused to provide additional details. It's unknown when the weapons were put into orbit.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

If the disclosure is meant to serve as a deterrent — aiming to warn adversaries that the US is capable of forcefully responding to threats in space — the vagueness of Meink's remarks may limit their effectiveness, said Clayton Swope, the deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the bipartisan nonprofit Center for Strategic and International Studies, who previously served for more than a decade in the CIA.

"The disclosure is still significant because it's not something that we have talked about in this way," Swope said. But "you really have to think out this chain of logic beyond just this disclosure."

For such a disclosure to be an effective deterrent, Swope said, US adversaries have to understand "what exactly is the destructive potential of this weapon, and then what exactly don't we want them to do — so that by knowing that they don't do it."

Militarizing space

President Donald Trump has touted the US Space Force, which he created in 2019 under the Department of the Air Force, as a historic step toward bolstering the nation's defense capabilities amid an advancing arms race in which China and Russia have challenged America's dominance in space.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"China develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," the US Space Force says on its website, while "Russia views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts."

US military officials have repeatedly warned the two countries are testing new offensive space capabilities, citing examples such as Russian satellite constellation training missions that Washington says could demonstrate "attack and defend tactics" for future combat and China's development of a nuclear capable partial-orbit hypersonic missile.

While the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons or weapons of mass destruction in orbit, it does not prohibit the use of conventional weapons in space or the use of ground-based weapons against assets in space — leaving room for interpretation.

It's not clear what type of weapon the US may have deployed. There are a broad range of possibilities — including satellites capable of jamming enemy communications and weapons that could leave orbit, target and destroy ground-based equipment, Swope said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It's even possible Meink could have been referring to an anti-satellite weapon, or ASAT, which can be used to seek out and physically destroy an enemy satellite in orbit.

Such technology has been previously tested by the US, China and Russia. But it's widely considered among the most risky and broadly detrimental types of space weapons because debris from exploded satellites can linger in orbit for years — risking setting off an indiscriminate string of collisions with any nearby satellites.

CNN has reached out to the Space Force for comment.

The US committed in 2022 to never again test "direct-ascent" ASAT weaponry, Swope noted, referring to types of ASAT weapons that are launched from the ground to target a satellite.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But the precise language of the commitment does not rule out testing or deploying another type of ASAT weapon, such as a "co-orbital" ASAT weapon, Swope said. That type of tool could involve using a spacecraft to directly approach an enemy satellite in orbit.

"Dating back to the Soviet Union and the Cold War, the Russians have been interested in developing what I would call 'co-orbital, anti-satellite' weapons," Swope added. "These are satellites that would launch some type of projectile or other munition at the target satellite to disable it."

'Maintain our dominance'

As CNN reported in 2024, US intelligence suggests Russia has also made efforts to develop a space-based nuclear weapon that would use a massive energy wave, known as an electromagnetic pulse, to potentially knock out a large swath of commercial and government satellites — a claim Moscow has denied.

Such a weapon could have broad, devastating impacts, such as upending satellites the world relies on to predict the weather and respond to disasters, or even potentially affecting global navigation systems used for a wide variety of purposes, including banking, cargo shipping, ambulance dispatch and even hailing a ride share.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

unknown content item

-

"It is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space, and so we've had to take steps to make sure that when we're threatened, we can take care of that," Meink said Monday.

Last December, Trump signed an executive order calling US superiority in space "a measure of national vision and willpower," with an emphasis on developing next-generation missile defense technologies and ensuring its abilities to counter threats, including "any placement of nuclear weapons in space."

The executive order was a step toward Trump's proposed "Golden Dome" missile defense system, an ambitious multibillion-dollar plan inspired by Israel's Iron Dome that officials say would allow the US to intercept missiles from anywhere in the world.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The US has remained vague on its plans for developing the missile shield, which Trump said he hopes will be completed by 2028. As CNN previously reported, the Pentagon has scheduled the shield's first major test for just before the 2028 election, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Among other elements, the Golden Dome proposal includes deploying interceptors that could remain in Earth orbit until they're used to destroy enemy missiles mid-flight.

Speaking Monday, Meink also said a US space-based interceptor program had moved "from initial contract to flight-ready hardware in less than one year," without revealing further details.

CNN's Rashard Rose, Simone McCarthy, Natasha Bertrand and Zachary Cohen contributed to this report.

data.title: Two House Democrats defect again on key vote for Trump agenda
data.description:
Two House Democrats defect again on key vote for Trump agenda

Sarah Ferris, CNN
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:22 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

House Democrats are fuming after a pair of centrist members once again defied their party leaders by voting to help advance a key White House priority — the second time in recent weeks.

The frustrations at those two Democrats — in particular, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who is seeking reelection in a battleground seat — are so high that they led to a confrontation on the House floor Tuesday evening between the Washington congresswoman and a top party leader, according to a person familiar with the exchange.

Rep. Katherine Clark, the No. 2 House Democrat and party whip, appeared to raise her voice in an intense conversation on the floor with Gluesenkamp Perez shortly after the vote, that person said. (The other Democratic defector, Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, is retiring after his term and has faced less party blowback.)

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The vote the two Democrats defected on is known as a rule vote. Typically, members of the minority party stick together to oppose these kind of procedural votes, which the majority party needs to bring bills to the floor.

Democrats are particularly irate given that one of the bills that can now be brought to the floor is a Russian sanctions bill that President Donald Trump himself has championed. The White House has made it such a high priority that some in the administration privately reached out to at least one House Democratic centrist, attempting to convince that member to support the GOP procedural vote in exchange for a community project back home, that member told CNN. That member ultimately opposed the GOP procedural vote.

While some Democrats support the Russia sanctions bill, they said they were not willing to back a GOP rule — and cross party leadership — to get that result.

The decision by the two Democrats to once again flout their leadership has quickly resurfaced a complicated debate about party discipline within the caucus. Democrats had already been discussing ways to punish members who oppose the party on key procedural votes after the last episode. Now, in the final week of session before the midterms, those conversations are quickly heating up.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Another top Democrat, Rep. Pete Aguilar, later called out the two defectors and said their caucus would discuss potential punishments for the members.

Asked about enforcing party discipline, he said, "We'll have some conversations as a family, and we'll go from there."

And he issued a terse warning to fellow Democrats about the behavior: "That's not what we should be doing."

data.title: Rubio announces US visa curbs for some foreign nationals from South Africa
data.description:
Rubio announces US visa curbs for some foreign nationals from South Africa

By Kanishka Singh and Bhargav Acharya
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:39 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Kanishka Singh and Bhargav Acharya

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday the U.S. was announcing a new visa restriction policy ‌targeting some foreign nationals from South Africa as President Donald Trump's administration continues ‌to cool ties with the country.

The Trump administration has criticized South Africa over a range of issues including actions ​aimed at addressing racial inequality that Trump claims hurt the African nation's white population.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Washington has also criticized land reform policies and South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, over the U.S. ally's assault on Gaza.

The visa curb policy targets "foreign nationals who are ‌responsible for, or complicit in, ⁠the enactment or implementation of laws or policies that enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and/or the incitement of imminent violence against members of ⁠minority ethnic or racial groups in South Africa," Rubio said in a statement.

"The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid out concerns," Rubio said.

The South African embassy in Washington did ​not ​immediately respond to a request for comment.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Pretoria says ​there is no evidence of discrimination ‌or persecution against white people and that ideas of white racial superiority are a threat to South Africa's post-apartheid unity, its sovereignty and its diplomatic relations. President Cyril Ramaphosa has called for global efforts to debunk false stories about white persecution.

Trump has previously cut aid to South Africa, offered refuge to white minority Afrikaners, expelled the country's ambassador and made false ‌claims of white genocide in the African nation.

Trump's portrayal ​of South Africa as dangerous and oppressive for white ​people also aligns with some of ​his domestic policies that have targeted diversity initiatives aimed at addressing historic ‌inequities for marginalized groups. Trump casts them ​as discriminatory against white ​people and men.

Rubio's statement on Tuesday did not identify any person by name.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Three decades after the end of apartheid in South Africa, some fringe groups lament the loss ​of white power that ‌democracy brought. While South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the ​world, most victims are Black.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh, Bhargav Acharya and Costas ​Pitas; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Nia Williams)

data.title: Haze in S’pore: Air quality improving; only central region remains in the unhealthy range
data.description:
Haze in S’pore: Air quality improving; only central region remains in the unhealthy range

Lim Ruey Yan
Updated Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:17 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE - The air quality in Singapore continued to improve early on Sept 16, with the 24-hour PSI in four of the five regions resting in the moderate range. At 6am, only the central region remains at 103, above the 101 threshold that marks an unhealthy quality on the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI). The central region includes the Thomson, Marymount, Sin Ming, Ang Mo Kio, Bishan, Serangoon Gardens, MacRitchie and Toa Payoh areas, according to the National Environment Agency (NEA) website.

The PSI stood at 87 for the east, 86 for the west, 78 for the north and 76 for the south at 6am on Sept 16.

This is in stark contrast to the day before, when unhealthy levels of pollutants were recorded all across the country, a first since September 2019.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Air quality is considered unhealthy when the 24-hour PSI is in the range of 101 to 200, during which the NEA advises the public to reduce outdoor activities. PSI readings of 51 to 100 are considered moderate, while values of zero to 50 are in the "good" range.The conditions on Sept 15 prompted some organisations such as the Football Association of Singapore to implement measures to mitigate the impact of the haze.

In an advisory on Sept 15, NEA said air quality in Singapore for the next 24 hours was forecast to be in the high moderate to mid-unhealthy range.

Dry conditions are expected over central and southern Sumatra and southern Kalimantan in neighbouring Indonesia - where forest fires have raged for weeks - in the coming days, NEA added.

"With the prevailing winds forecast to continue blowing from the south-east to east-south-east, there is a risk of smoke haze affecting Singapore," the agency said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The PSI crossed into the unhealthy range two weeks ago, hitting 101 in central Singapore on the morning of Sept 4. In the days that followed, readings in the central, eastern and western parts of Singapore occasionally crossed into the unhealthy range.September's developments mark the first time since October 2023 that the PSI in Singapore hit unhealthy levels because of haze, with the authorities earlier warning of the risk of haze between June and October as a result of warmer and drier conditions brought on by both El Nino and the Indian Ocean Dipole.

data.title: Internet connection for about 2,000 in Bishan, Thomson restored: NetLink Trust
data.description:
Internet connection for about 2,000 in Bishan, Thomson restored: NetLink Trust

Lim Ruey Yan
Updated Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:07 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE - Fibre services in parts of Bishan and Thomson that were disrupted on Sept 15 have been restored, said NetLink Trust in a statement on Sept 16.It added that the disruption, which affected about 2,000 connections, was caused by damage to NetLink's fibre infrastructure during construction works carried out by a third-party contractor. NetLink Trust designs, builds, owns and operates the passive fibre network infrastructure of Singapore's Nationwide Broadband Network.

"We are conducting a thorough review of the incident and will take appropriate follow-up actions upon completion of our investigations," it said in a statement on its website at 6am, noting that works were completed at 5.40am.

"Our teams worked continuously through the night to restore affected services as quickly and safely as possible.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"We sincerely apologise for the disruption and inconvenience caused and thank affected end users for their patience and understanding."

It advised end users who continue to experience service issues to contact their respective Internet Service Providers for further assistance.Reports of the disruption first surfaced on DownDetector - a website that tracks service disruptions - just after lunch on Sept 15.

In an update at 9.45pm, it said recovery efforts were complicated by conditions at the damage site, including water ingress and obstructions that were limiting access to the underground cables.

It added then that its teams would be working through the night to repair the damaged cables.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In separate social media posts on Sept 15, telcos Singtel, StarHub and M1 said the outage may have affected some of their subscribers.

StarHub said in a Facebook post that the disruption was due to a "fibre cut", while Singtel separately said on the social networking platform that it was informed by NetLink Trust of the outage in Bishan.

In an update at around 7.20pm, Singtel added that its mobile services are not affected by the outage and are operating normally.

NetLink Trust previously experienced a fibre service outage in April, during which 5,000 broadband connections in central and north-east Singapore were affected for around 20 hours.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The cable damage also affected the Expected Time of Arrival system for buses, and led to the system displaying inaccurate bus timings and long wait times at bus stops and on mobile apps.

The Land Transport Authority said then that the fibre service cables were damaged during construction works for the North-South Corridor project.

data.title: Trump threatens to keep Kennedy Center shut if his name not added
data.description:
Trump threatens to keep Kennedy Center shut if his name not added

Danny KEMP and Daniel STUBLEN
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:18 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

US President Donald Trump threatened Tuesday to keep the Kennedy Center closed for good after a judge ruled his name cannot be added onto the famed arts institution's facade.

Trump said his hand-picked board voted "almost unanimously" to shut the venue immediately for emergency renovations, just a few hours after the federal judge's decision.

But he warned the "very large and complex" repairs at the building in Washington cannot begin until a higher court rules on whether the center can be renamed after himself.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

The Kennedy Center said in a statement to AFP that the board's decision "reflects sound judgment and a clear prioritization of safety above all else."

Shortly after beginning his second term, Republican Trump installed himself as chairman of the center, which is named in honor of late president John F. Kennedy, a Democrat who championed civil rights before he was assassinated in 1963.

The board voted in December to call it the "Trump-Kennedy" Center and installed signage with his name on it.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

US federal judge Christopher Cooper previously ordered Trump's name removed from the exterior and overturned the board's decision to rename the institution.

Cooper ruled on Tuesday that Trump's name cannot be added back, rebuking the center for trying to circumvent his earlier order.

"Simply put," wrote Cooper in his decision, the board "cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."

- Demolition threat -

Trump himself called into the board meeting and berated a Democratic congresswoman who serves on the board and filed the lawsuit that blocked its renaming, CNN reported.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Kennedy Center takeover is one of several projects aimed at stamping Trump's brand on the US capital, including a triumphal arch and a half-billion dollar ballroom at the White House.

Workers removed Trump's name from the building in June, but scaffolding and tarps have remained ever since.

Last month, the board moved forward with a plan to add a new signage on the building that would read "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump."

Cooper on Tuesday said that plan was in violation of his previous ruling.

Trump and his chosen leaders of the Kennedy Center have argued that its main building, which was constructed in the 1960s, is in a state of dangerous disrepair.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

As evidence of the safety problems, the president pointed to a recent incident in which a piece of the ceiling tumbled to the ground following a storm.

"If the Building were open, innocent people would have been killed," he wrote in a post on Truth Social before the judge's ruling.

Last month, as part of court proceedings, the Trump administration warned that the center may need to be demolished, if its plans to renovate the building were blocked.

A host of artists canceled concerts at the venue in response to Trump's takeover, while US media has reported that Kennedy Center ticket sales have plummeted.

data.title: Former Philippines leader Duterte due in ICC courtroom to assess if fit for murder trial
data.description:
Former Philippines leader Duterte due in ICC courtroom to assess if fit for murder trial

By Anthony Deutsch
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:01 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Anthony Deutsch

THE HAGUE, Netherlands, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte is expected to appear in public for ‌the first time on Wednesday since being transferred to the ‌International Criminal Court 18 months ago to face murder charges related to his war ​on drugs.

Duterte, 81, served as president from 2016 to 2022, before being charged with crimes against humanity for creating, funding and arming death squads that targeted narcotics peddlers and users. He was arrested and taken ‌to The Hague in ⁠March 2025.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

On Wednesday, judges will hear arguments about his health and ability to stand trial, which is scheduled ⁠to begin in November. His lawyers have argued that he suffers from cognitive decline and is not well enough.

Duterte's lawyer and family did not ​respond to ​requests for comment.

ICC judges said ​in January that Duterte's health ‌was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court, rather than by video link from the detention unit.

Duterte's warrant says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including ‌when he served as mayor of ​the southern Davao city.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

ICC prosecutors have said ​as many as 30,000 people ​may have been killed in the crackdown, the details ‌of which were reported in a Reuters ​investigation.

According to police, ​6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations. Duterte said he instructed police to act in self-defence and told supporters he was ready ​to "rot in jail" if ‌it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs.

data.title: US House committee recommends contempt of Congress for Leon Black in Epstein probe
data.description:
US House committee recommends contempt of Congress for Leon Black in Epstein probe

By Isla Binnie and Nolan D. McCaskill
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 10:09 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Isla Binnie and Nolan D. McCaskill

NEW YORK, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The U.S. House of Representatives Oversight Committee voted to recommend holding ‌Leon Black in contempt of Congress on Tuesday, after the Wall ‌Street billionaire declined to comply with subpoenas as part of a probe into the activities of ​late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Black, who co-founded private equity giant Apollo Global Management, is among several prominent political and business figures who have been called to testify about their ties to the late financier.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The 41-0 committee vote sets up ‌a vote by the full ⁠House to refer the case to the Justice Department for possible prosecution under a simple majority threshold. Contempt of Congress ⁠is a misdemeanor charge that carries up to a year in prison and a fine of up to $100,000.

Black gave up his role as Apollo chief executive ​in 2021 ​after an external law firm found he ​had paid Epstein $158 million for ‌tax and estate planning.

He sued the committee this month and declined to appear at a deposition. The deposition was scheduled after a voluntary appearance in June during which Black told the committee he never abused women or engaged in sex trafficking and had never had sex with underage women. He denies ‌knowledge of Epstein's conduct.

He walked out during ​the June interview, according to members of the ​committee, who ordered him to ​come back to testify under oath and then issued subpoenas ‌for documents.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Black's lawyers said on Tuesday ​the contempt resolution ​showed the committee had "lost sight of its legislative purpose and (was) abusing its power", adding they had written to ask the Office of Congressional Conduct ​to investigate Comer.

Epstein was ‌found dead in a New York City jail cell in 2019, ​and his death was ruled a suicide.
